title: Malaysia: Coalition Politics, Political Transitions, and Post-2018 Electoral Change
topic: Malaysia: coalition politics, political transitions, and post-2018 electoral change
abstract: This synthetic research outline covers Malaysia's post-2018 federal political change, focusing on coalition bargaining after GE14, the 2020 Sheraton Move, pandemic-era government turnover, and the hung parliament that followed GE15. It treats electoral change as a shift from dominant-party rule to coalition bargaining, with defections, regional blocs, and anti-hopping reforms shaping outcomes. The set is designed for stable benchmark generation and keeps PDF-facing text in English with selected Malay and Simplified Chinese markers for extraction clarity.

sections.heading: The 2018 Election and the End of BN's Dominance
bullet_points: Place GE14 in 2018 at the center of the break from uninterrupted Barisan Nasional federal rule.
Explain that Pakatan Harapan won power through a broad anti-incumbent coalition rather than a single-party sweep.
Treat Mahathir Mohamad's return as prime minister as part of a coalition bargain, not as a simple restoration of old politics.
Keep the section focused on the federal breakthrough and the new electoral baseline it created.

sections.heading: Coalition Bargaining Inside Pakatan Harapan
bullet_points: Describe Pakatan Harapan as a coalition with internal balance problems, not a monolithic governing machine.
Show how disagreements over leadership succession, institutional reform, and alliance discipline created pressure inside the coalition.
Explain why Bersatu's position inside PH mattered so much for the durability of the 2018 settlement.
Keep the section on the mechanics of coalition bargaining rather than on the later collapse itself.

sections.heading: The Sheraton Move and the 2020 Government Reset
bullet_points: Treat the Sheraton Move as the turning point that converted coalition strain into a federal government reset.
Explain that defections, party withdrawals, and royal appointment procedures mattered more than a fresh general election.
Describe the shift from a PH-led cabinet to a Muhyiddin-led coalition as a parliamentary realignment.
Keep the section anchored in February and March 2020, with the pandemic only as background context.

sections.heading: Pandemic Rule, Party Defections, and Institutional Repair
bullet_points: Explain how pandemic-era governance intensified the importance of parliamentary majority testing and elite bargaining.
Show why Muhyiddin's government became vulnerable once UMNO support thinned and defections continued.
Describe the 2021 shift to Ismail Sabri as a coalition compromise built on narrower support but broader cross-bloc tolerance.
Use this section to connect political instability to the later anti-hopping reform agenda.

sections.heading: GE15, Hung Parliament, and the New Coalition Equilibrium
bullet_points: Describe GE15 in 2022 as the moment when no bloc secured a simple majority and coalition bargaining became unavoidable.
Explain Anwar Ibrahim's eventual appointment as prime minister as the outcome of post-election coalition assembly, not a single-party mandate.
Show how regional blocs such as GPS and other cross-party alignments became decisive in the final settlement.
Frame the new equilibrium as a normalized coalition era shaped by hung parliament arithmetic and anti-hopping rules.
